fis-01-cinematica.title: Kinematics: launching a projectile
fis-01-cinematica.theory:
# What is kinematics?

**Kinematics** describes **how** things move, without asking **why** yet (that is dynamics, in the next lesson). It uses three quantities:

- **Position** `x` — where the body is, in metres (m).
- **Velocity** `v = Δx / Δt` — how much the position changes per second (m/s).
- **Acceleration** `a = Δv / Δt` — how much the velocity changes per second (m/s²).

## Uniformly accelerated motion

When the acceleration is constant, three equations hold that you will use for the rest of your life:

```
v = v0 + a·t
x = x0 + v0·t + a·t²/2
v² = v0² + 2·a·Δx        (Torricelli)
```

Near the Earth's surface, every body in free fall has the same downward acceleration: **g ≈ 9.81 m/s²** — a stone and a feather fall together in a vacuum!

# Projectile motion

Galileo's trick: **split the motion in two**. A cannon fires the ball with speed `v0` at an angle `θ`:

- **Horizontally** nothing pushes or slows the ball: constant velocity `vx = v0·cos θ`.
- **Vertically** it slows down on the way up and speeds up on the way down, with `a = −g`: it starts with `vy = v0·sin θ`.

```
x(t) = v0·cos θ · t
y(t) = h0 + v0·sin θ · t − g·t²/2
```

Launching from the ground (`h0 = 0`) and solving `y = 0`:

```
flight time:   T = 2·v0·sin θ / g
range:         R = v0²·sin(2θ) / g
max height:    H = (v0·sin θ)² / (2·g)
```

## What the range teaches

- `sin(2θ)` is largest when `2θ = 90°`: **45° gives the longest range** (without air).
- **Complementary** angles (30° and 60°, 20° and 70°) give the **same range** — but the higher one stays in the air much longer.
- Doubling the speed **quadruples** the range (`v0²`).

## Model assumptions

- No air resistance (we will add air in the last lesson).
- Constant `g` and a flat Earth — fine for ranges of a few kilometres.
- The ball is a point: it doesn't spin and has no size.
fis-01-cinematica.task: Hit the green flag **30 m** away (the ball must land between 29 and 31 m) with a **flight time under 3 s**. Change the speed and the angle and click **▶ Run** for each try.
hints: From the ground, the range is `R = v0²·sin(2θ)/g`. At 45°, `sin 90° = 1`, so `R = v0²/g`.
High angles like 60° also hit, but the ball climbs a lot and takes more than 3 s: stick to angles up to 45°.
goals: The ball lands on the target (30 m ± 1 m)
Flight time under 3 s

questions.prompt: A ball rolls off a table and falls from a height of **20 m** (no air, g = 9.8 m/s²). How long does it take to reach the ground?
questions.explanation: Vertically it starts from rest: 20 = 9.8·t²/2 → t = √(40/9.8) ≈ 2.02 s. The horizontal speed doesn't change that time!

questions.prompt: Without air resistance, launching from the ground, which angle gives the **longest range**?
questions.explanation: The range is v0²·sin(2θ)/g, largest when sin(2θ) = 1, that is, 2θ = 90° → θ = 45°.

questions.prompt: A car starts from rest with a constant acceleration of **3 m/s²**. What is its speed after **4 s**?

fis-02-newton.title: Newton's laws: the block on the ramp
fis-02-newton.theory:
# Newton's three laws

Kinematics tells how something moves; **dynamics** tells why. It all fits in three laws:

- **1st law (inertia):** if the net force is zero, a body stays at rest or keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed.
- **2nd law:** the net force produces acceleration: `F_net = m·a`. Force in **newtons** (N), mass in kg.
- **3rd law (action and reaction):** if A pushes B, B pushes A with an equal and opposite force — on **different** bodies, which is why they don't cancel out.

# The forces that show up in almost every problem

- **Weight** `P = m·g` — the Earth pulls the block down (5 kg → 49 N).
- **Normal** `N` — the surface pushes the block, always **perpendicular** to it.
- **Friction** — always **against** the motion (or against the tendency to move):
  - at rest: static friction adjusts itself, up to a maximum `f ≤ μ·N`;
  - sliding: kinetic friction `f = μ·N`.

## Splitting the weight on a ramp

On a ramp at angle `θ`, use axes **along** and **perpendicular to** the ramp:

```
P parallel      = m·g·sin θ  (down the ramp)
P perpendicular = m·g·cos θ  (into the ramp)
N               = m·g·cos θ
```

Along the ramp, with a force `F` pulling up and the block moving up:

```
F − m·g·sin θ − μ·m·g·cos θ = m·a
```

## Example

A 5 kg block, 30° ramp, μ = 0.2, no applied force: `P parallel = 24.5 N` and the maximum friction is `0.2 · 42.5 = 8.5 N`. Since 24.5 > 8.5, it **slides down** with `a = (24.5 − 8.5)/5 ≈ 3.2 m/s²`.

## Simulator assumptions

- `g = 9.81 m/s²`; the block is rigid and starts at rest in the middle of the ramp.
- A single μ is used for static and kinetic friction (in real life the static one is usually a bit larger).
- The applied force is parallel to the ramp (positive = up the ramp). The diagram on the right shows every force (mg = weight, f = friction).
fis-02-newton.task: The block has **5 kg** and the friction is **μ = 0.2** (locked). Choose the force so that it moves **up** the ramp with an acceleration between **1.8 and 2.2 m/s²**, on a ramp of **at least 30°**.
hints: Add up the forces along the ramp: `F − P·sin θ − f = m·a`.
goals: The block moves up with an acceleration between 1.8 and 2.2 m/s²
Ramp inclined at least 30°

questions.prompt: A **5 kg** block rests on a **30°** ramp (g = 9.8 m/s²). What is the normal force?
questions.explanation: N = m·g·cos θ = 5·9.8·0.866 ≈ 42.4 N. The normal force is smaller than the weight (49 N) because it only balances the part of the weight perpendicular to the ramp.

questions.prompt: By Newton's 3rd law, what is the **reaction** to the block's weight (the Earth pulling the block)?
options: The normal force the ramp exerts on the block
The force with which the block pulls the Earth upward
The friction between the block and the ramp
There is no reaction to the weight
questions.explanation: Action and reaction are of the same kind and act on different bodies: the Earth attracts the block and the block attracts the Earth with the same force. The normal force is NOT the reaction to the weight.

questions.prompt: With **μ = 0.5**, what is the **steepest** ramp angle at which a block stays at rest on its own?
questions.explanation: At the limit, m·g·sin θ = μ·m·g·cos θ → tan θ = μ = 0.5 → θ ≈ 26.6°. Notice the mass doesn't even enter the calculation!

fis-03-energia.title: Energy and work: the spring launcher
fis-03-energia.theory:
# Work: a force along a path

A force **does work** when it moves something:

```
W = F·d·cos θ        (joules: 1 J = 1 N·m)
```

`θ` is the angle between the force and the displacement. Pushing along the motion gives **positive** work; friction, which acts against it, gives **negative** work; the normal force, being perpendicular, does no work at all.

# Forms of energy

- **Kinetic** (motion): `KE = m·v²/2`
- **Gravitational potential** (height): `PE = m·g·h`
- **Elastic potential** (stretched or compressed spring): `Ee = k·x²/2`

## Work–energy theorem

The **total** work on a body becomes a change in its kinetic energy: `W_total = ΔKE`.

## Conservation of mechanical energy

Without friction or air resistance, energy only **changes form** — the sum stays constant:

```
KE + PE + Ee = constant
```

# The spring (Hooke's law)

A spring pulls back in proportion to how much it was deformed: `F = −k·x`. The **spring constant** `k` (N/m) tells how stiff it is.

In the lab the block is pulled to `x = A` and released. There all the energy is elastic; when it passes `x = 0` all of it has become kinetic:

```
k·A²/2 = m·v_max²/2   →   v_max = A·√(k/m)
```

The bars show the energy flowing from elastic to kinetic and back, with a constant total.

## Power

`P = W / Δt` (watts). A 100 W motor delivers 100 J every second.

## Simulator assumptions

- Ideal, massless spring; frictionless floor; rigid block.
fis-03-energia.task: Build a spring launcher that gives the block a **maximum speed between 3.8 and 4.2 m/s** while storing **at most 10 J** in the spring.
hints: The maximum speed is `v_max = A·√(k/m)` and the stored energy is `E = k·A²/2 = m·v_max²/2`.
At v = 4 m/s the energy is `8·m`: to stay under 10 J, the mass must be at most 1.25 kg.
Example: m = 1 kg, k = 200 N/m and A = 0.28 m → v_max ≈ 3.96 m/s and E ≈ 7.8 J.
goals: Maximum speed between 3.8 and 4.2 m/s
Energy stored in the spring of at most 10 J

questions.prompt: A spring with **k = 400 N/m** is compressed by **0.1 m**. How much energy does it store?
A **2 kg** block slides without friction from a height of **5 m** (g = 9.8 m/s²). How fast is it at the bottom?
questions.explanation: m·g·h = m·v²/2 → v = √(2·g·h) = √98 ≈ 9.9 m/s. The mass cancels out!

questions.prompt: A box is dragged 3 m across the floor. The work done on it by the **friction force** is…
options: negative, because friction opposes the displacement
equal to the work done by the weight
questions.explanation: W = F·d·cos 180° = −F·d: friction takes kinetic energy from the body and turns it into heat.

fis-04-colisoes.title: Momentum and collisions
fis-04-colisoes.theory:
# Momentum (linear momentum)

A truck at 10 km/h is harder to stop than a bicycle at the same speed. The quantity that measures this is **momentum**:

```
p = m·v        (kg·m/s, it is a vector: it has a direction!)
```

## Impulse

A force acting for some time changes the momentum: `I = F·Δt = Δp`. That's why airbags save lives: they **lengthen the time** of the stop, lowering the force.

# Conservation of momentum

If no **external** force acts on the system, the total momentum doesn't change — even in a violent crash, because the forces between the carts are action and reaction (3rd law) and cancel out in the total:

```
m1·v1 + m2·v2 = m1·v1' + m2·v2'
```

## Kinds of collision

Momentum is **always** conserved; kinetic energy **not always**. The **coefficient of restitution** measures how fast the bodies separate afterwards compared with how fast they approached before:

```
e = (v2' − v1') / (v1 − v2)
```

- `e = 1` — **elastic**: kinetic energy is also conserved (billiard balls, almost).
- `0 < e < 1` — **partially inelastic**: part of the energy becomes heat, sound, deformation.
- `e = 0` — **perfectly inelastic**: the bodies stick together and move as one. It loses the most energy.

Combining the two equations, the velocities afterwards are:

```
v1' = (m1·v1 + m2·v2 + m2·e·(v2 − v1)) / (m1 + m2)
v2' = (m1·v1 + m2·v2 + m1·e·(v1 − v2)) / (m1 + m2)
```

## Simulator assumptions

- Straight, frictionless track (the only horizontal force is the one of the crash).
- Instantaneous collision, in one dimension. Positive velocity = to the right.
fis-04-colisoes.task: Recreate the famous **Newton's cradle**: make cart 1 **stop completely** after the crash, handing all its motion to cart 2, **without losing kinetic energy** (at most 1% lost).
hints: To lose no energy, the collision must be elastic: `e = 1`.
In an elastic collision between **equal** masses, the carts simply swap velocities.
Example: m1 = m2 = 2 kg, v1 = 2 m/s, v2 = 0 and e = 1.
goals: The carts collide
Cart 1 stops after the crash (|v1'| ≤ 0.05 m/s)
Kinetic energy conserved (at most 1% lost)

questions.prompt: A **2 kg** cart moving at **3 m/s** hits a **1 kg** cart at rest and the two **stick together**. What is the speed of the pair?
questions.explanation: Momentum before: 2·3 = 6 kg·m/s. After: (2 + 1)·v = 6 → v = 2 m/s.

questions.prompt: In the crash of the previous question, how much **kinetic energy was lost**?
questions.explanation: Before: 2·3²/2 = 9 J. After: 3·2²/2 = 6 J. 3 J were lost, turned into heat, sound and deformation.

questions.prompt: In a collision where no external force acts, what is **always** conserved?
questions.explanation: Total momentum is always conserved without external forces. Kinetic energy is only conserved in elastic collisions.

fis-05-orbitas.title: Circular motion and gravitation: a satellite in orbit
fis-05-orbitas.theory:
# Circular motion

A body going around a circle at constant speed **is accelerating**: the direction of its velocity changes all the time. That acceleration points to the centre (**centripetal**):

```
v  = 2·π·r / T          (T = period)
ω  = 2·π / T = v / r    (angular velocity, rad/s)
ac = v² / r = ω²·r
```

By the 2nd law, some force must pull towards the centre: `Fc = m·v²/r`. For a car on a bend it is the tyres' friction; for a stone on a string, the tension; for a satellite, **gravity**.

# Universal gravitation

Newton realised that the force that makes the apple fall is the same one that holds the Moon:

```
F = G·M·m / r²        G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²
```

`r` is the distance between the **centres**. For the Earth, `G·M ≈ 398 600 km³/s²`.

## Newton's cannon

Imagine a cannon on top of a mountain. The faster the ball leaves, the farther it lands — until, at a certain speed, the Earth "curves away" exactly as much as the ball falls: it **falls forever around the Earth**. That's an orbit! Setting gravity equal to the centripetal force:

```
G·M·m/r² = m·v²/r
v_circular = √(G·M / r)
T = 2·π·√(r³ / (G·M))    (Kepler: T² ∝ r³)
v_escape = √(2·G·M / r) = √2 · v_circular
```

## Elliptical orbits

- Slower than `v_circular`: the orbit becomes an **ellipse** that dips down (and may hit the planet).
- Faster: an ellipse that rises to a distant **apogee**.
- From `v_escape` on: the satellite **escapes** and never comes back.

The **eccentricity** `e` measures how flattened it is: 0 = circle, close to 1 = a very stretched ellipse.

## Simulator assumptions

- Spherical planet, no atmosphere and no other bodies (Moon, Sun).
- Horizontal launch (perpendicular to the radius). Altitude = distance above the surface.
fis-05-orbitas.task: Put a satellite into a **circular orbit at 400 km** of altitude, like the International Space Station: it must neither fall nor escape, the eccentricity must be **at most 0.01** and the period between **90 and 95 minutes**.
hints: Use `v = √(G·M/r)` with `r` measured from the **centre** of the Earth: r = 6371 + 400 = 6771 km.
If the satellite falls, increase the speed; if the orbit stretches too much, decrease it. Fine-tune in steps of 0.01 km/s.
goals: The satellite stays in orbit (doesn't fall or escape)
Nearly circular orbit (eccentricity ≤ 0.01)
Period between 90 and 95 minutes
Launched at 400 km of altitude (between 390 and 410 km)

questions.prompt: What would be the speed of a **grazing** circular orbit around the Moon (r = 1737 km, G·M = 4903 km³/s²)?
questions.explanation: v = √(G·M/r) = √(4903/1737) ≈ 1.68 km/s — much less than on Earth, because the Moon has much less mass.

questions.prompt: Why do astronauts **float** inside the Space Station, only 400 km up?
options: Because there is no gravity up there
Because they are in free fall together with the station
Because the air up there pushes them up
Because the Moon pulls them the other way
questions.explanation: At 400 km gravity is still ~89% of the surface value! The station and the astronauts fall together around the Earth, so nothing presses the astronauts against the floor.

questions.prompt: A car takes a bend of radius **50 m** at **20 m/s**. What is the centripetal acceleration?
questions.explanation: ac = v²/r = 400/50 = 8 m/s² — almost 1 g! The tyres' friction provides that force.

fis-06-pendulo.title: Oscillations: the pendulum that beats seconds
fis-06-pendulo.theory:
# Simple harmonic motion (SHM)

Lots of things **go back and forth**: a swing, a guitar string, atoms in a crystal, electric circuits. When the restoring force is proportional to the displacement (`F = −k·x`), the motion is **SHM**:

```
x(t) = A·cos(ω·t)
T = 2·π / ω        (period, s)
f = 1 / T          (frequency, Hz)
```

For the **mass–spring** system: `ω = √(k/m)`, so `T = 2·π·√(m/k)`.

# The simple pendulum

A mass hanging from a string of length `L`. The part of the weight that pulls it back is `m·g·sin θ`, and the equation of motion is:

```
θ'' = −(g/L)·sin θ
```

For **small angles** (up to about 15°), `sin θ ≈ θ` (in radians) and it becomes SHM:

```
T = 2·π·√(L / g)
```

## Surprising facts

- The period **doesn't depend on the mass**: lead or styrofoam, same period.
- For small swings it also **doesn't depend on the amplitude** (isochronism, discovered by Galileo watching a chandelier in a church). That's why the pendulum became a clock.
- For large amplitudes the period **grows**: `T ≈ T0·(1 + θ0²/16)` with θ0 in radians — at 40° it is about 3% longer.
- On the Moon (g = 1.62 m/s²) the same pendulum swings ~2.5 times slower.

## Damping and resonance

Air friction makes the amplitude shrink little by little (**damping**). Pushing at the right rhythm — at the natural frequency — makes the amplitude grow a lot: that's **resonance**, which you use on a playground swing.

## Simulator assumptions

- Point mass on a massless, inextensible string.
- The simulator solves the **full** equation (with `sin θ`) numerically, so it shows the effect of large amplitudes. The period is measured from the motion itself.
fis-06-pendulo.task: Build a **seconds pendulum** on Earth (each swing one way takes 1 s): period between **1.98 and 2.02 s**, with an amplitude of at most **15°** so the small-swing formula holds.
hints: Solve `T = 2·π·√(L/g)` for L: `L = g·(T / 2π)²`.
Use a small amplitude (5°, for example) and keep the planet on Earth.
goals: Period between 1.98 and 2.02 s
Amplitude of at most 15°
On Earth (g = 9.81 m/s²)

questions.prompt: What is the period of a **1 m** pendulum on the **Moon** (g = 1.62 m/s²), with small swings?
questions.explanation: T = 2π·√(1/1.62) ≈ 2π·0.786 ≈ 4.94 s — 2.5 times slower than on Earth (2.0 s).

questions.prompt: For small swings, what changes the period of a simple pendulum?
questions.explanation: T = 2π·√(L/g): only the length and gravity. The mass doesn't appear, and the amplitude only matters when it is large.

questions.prompt: A **0.5 kg** mass on a spring with **k = 200 N/m** oscillates. What is the period?

fis-07-optica.title: Waves and optics: forming images with lenses
fis-07-optica.theory:
# Waves

A **wave** carries energy without carrying matter: a stadium wave travels, the people stay in place. Every periodic wave obeys:

```
v = λ·f
```

- `λ` (lambda) — **wavelength**, the distance between two crests (m).
- `f` — **frequency**, how many crests pass per second (Hz).
- `v` — propagation speed: sound in air ≈ 340 m/s; light in vacuum `c ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s`.

Sound is a **mechanical** wave (it needs a medium). Light is an **electromagnetic** wave (it travels through vacuum); its colour depends on the wavelength: violet ~400 nm, red ~700 nm.

When two waves meet they add up (**interference**): crests with crests reinforce, crests with troughs cancel — that's what makes the colours on a soap bubble.

# Refraction

When light changes medium it changes speed and **bends** (Snell's law): `n1·sin θ1 = n2·sin θ2`, with `n = c / v` (refractive index; glass ≈ 1.5). Lenses use this to bend rays.

# Thin lenses

- **Converging** (thicker in the middle): brings parallel rays together at a **focus** F', at a distance `f`.
- **Diverging** (thinner in the middle): spreads the rays, as if they came from a virtual focus.

## The three principal rays

- Ray **parallel** to the axis → leaves through the focus F' (or away from F, for a diverging lens).
- Ray through the **centre** of the lens → goes straight through.
- Ray through the **focus** F → leaves parallel to the axis (for a diverging lens, the ray **aimed** at the focus on the other side).

Where the rays (or their extensions) cross, the **image** is formed.

## Thin lens equation and magnification

```
1/f = 1/do + 1/di
m = −di / do          (magnification)
```

- `di > 0`: **real** image (on the other side, it can be projected on a screen).
- `di < 0`: **virtual** image (on the same side, only seen through the lens — a magnifying glass).
- `m < 0`: **inverted** image; `|m| > 1`: larger than the object.
- Converging: `f > 0`; diverging: `f < 0`. Optical power `D = 1/f` in dioptres (f in metres) — the strength of glasses.

## Simulator assumptions

- Thin lens, rays close to the axis (paraxial approximation).
- In the drawing heights are magnified relative to distances, to keep it readable; the lines stay straight and cross in the right place.
fis-07-optica.task: With the **converging** lens, build a **projector**: form a **real, inverted image twice as large** as the object (magnification between −2.1 and −1.9).
hints: Magnification −2 means `di = 2·do` (real image, on the other side, twice as far).
In the lens equation: `1/f = 1/do + 1/(2·do) = 3/(2·do)` → `do = 1.5·f`.
With f = 10 cm, place the object 15 cm from the lens.
goals: The image is real (it forms on the other side of the lens)
Inverted image, twice as large (magnification between −2.1 and −1.9)

questions.prompt: A **680 Hz** sound travels in air at **340 m/s**. What is its wavelength?
A converging lens has **f = 20 cm** and the object is **60 cm** from it. How far from the lens does the image form?
questions.explanation: 1/di = 1/20 − 1/60 = 2/60 → di = 30 cm (real, inverted and half the size, m = −0.5).

questions.prompt: The image of a real object formed by a **diverging** lens is always…
questions.explanation: A diverging lens spreads the rays; their extensions cross on the object's side, closer to the lens: a virtual, upright and smaller image (like a door peephole).

fis-08-termodinamica.title: Thermodynamics: the ideal gas and the first law
fis-08-termodinamica.safety: Never heat **closed containers** (cans, jars, a pressure cooker with a clogged valve): by the gas law, the pressure rises with the temperature until the container explodes.
fis-08-termodinamica.theory:
# Temperature, pressure and the ideal gas

- **Temperature** measures how agitated the molecules are. In physics we use **kelvin**: `T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15`. Zero kelvin is absolute zero.
- **Pressure** is force per area: `p = F / A` (pascal, Pa = N/m²). Air at sea level pushes with ~101 kPa.
- 1 litre = 0.001 m³.

An **ideal gas** (point-like molecules that only bump into each other) follows:

```
p·V = n·R·T        R = 8.314 J/(mol·K)
```

In the lab the molecules (yellow dots) move faster when the gas heats up: the average speed grows with `√T`.

# Internal energy, heat and work

- **Internal energy** `U` — the energy of the molecules. In a monatomic ideal gas: `U = (3/2)·n·R·T` — it only depends on the temperature!
- **Heat** `Q` — energy that flows in because of a temperature difference (Q > 0 when entering).
- **Work** `W` — energy the gas delivers by pushing the piston. With varying pressure, `W` is the **area under the curve** on the p–V graph (W > 0 when the gas expands).

## First law (conservation of energy)

```
ΔU = Q − W
```

## The classic processes

- **Isothermal** (constant T): `ΔU = 0`, so `Q = W = n·R·T·ln(V2/V1)`. All the heat received becomes work.
- **Isobaric** (constant p): `W = p·(V2 − V1)`; the gas heats up as it expands.
- **Isochoric** (constant V): `W = 0`, all the heat becomes internal energy.
- **Adiabatic** (no heat exchanged, Q = 0): `p·V^γ` constant, with `γ = 5/3` for a monatomic gas; when it expands the gas **cools down** (`W = −ΔU`) — that's how rising air expands, cools and forms clouds.

# Second law and heat engines

Heat flows by itself from hot to cold, and no engine turns **all** the heat into work in a cycle. The limit is the **Carnot efficiency**:

```
η_max = 1 − T_cold / T_hot   (in kelvin)
```

## Simulator assumptions

- Monatomic ideal gas, slow (quasi-static) processes, frictionless piston.
fis-08-termodinamica.task: Start with **1 mol at 300 K in 10 L** (locked). Choose the process and the final volume so that the gas **does about 1000 J of work** (between 950 and 1050 J) **without changing its internal energy** (ΔU between −1 and 1 J).
hints: Constant internal energy means constant temperature: which process is that?
In the isothermal process, `W = n·R·T·ln(V2/V1)` and `n·R·T = 8.314·300 ≈ 2494 J`.
goals: The gas does between 950 and 1050 J of work
The internal energy doesn't change (ΔU between −1 and 1 J)

questions.prompt: What is the pressure of **1 mol** of ideal gas at **300 K** filling **24.9 L**?
questions.explanation: p = n·R·T / V = 8.314·300 / 0.0249 ≈ 100 200 Pa ≈ 100 kPa — practically atmospheric pressure.

questions.prompt: What is the **maximum efficiency** (Carnot) of an engine working between **600 K** and **300 K**?
questions.explanation: η = 1 − 300/600 = 0.5 = 50%. Real engines stay well below that.

questions.prompt: In an **adiabatic expansion**, what happens to the gas temperature?
options: It rises, because the volume increases
It stays the same, because no heat is exchanged
It drops, because the gas spends internal energy doing work
It depends on the colour of the container
questions.explanation: With Q = 0, ΔU = −W: the work of pushing the piston comes out of the internal energy, and the temperature drops.

fis-09-eletromagnetismo.title: Electricity and magnetism: charges, fields and currents
fis-09-eletromagnetismo.safety: Household mains (110–240 V) **kills**. Never touch live wires; electricity experiments are done with low-voltage cells and batteries.
fis-09-eletromagnetismo.theory:
# Electric charge and Coulomb's law

Matter has **positive** charges (protons) and **negative** ones (electrons). Like charges repel, opposite charges attract. Charge is measured in **coulombs** (C); an electron has a charge of `−1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C`.

```
F = k·|q1·q2| / r²        k ≈ 9×10⁹ N·m²/C²
```

Notice the similarity with gravitation: it also falls off as `1/r²`, but it is **much** stronger and can repel.

# Field and potential

- **Electric field** `E = F / q` (N/C or V/m): the force per unit charge at each point in space. Field lines leave positive charges and enter negative ones.
- **Potential** and **potential difference** (voltage) `U` in volts: energy per unit charge. A 1.5 V cell gives 1.5 J to each coulomb that passes.

# Current and circuits

- **Current** `I = ΔQ / Δt` (amperes): how much charge passes per second.
- **Ohm's law:** `U = R·I` (R in ohms, Ω).
- **Power:** `P = U·I = R·I² = U²/R` (watts).
- Resistors in **series** add up: `R = R1 + R2`. In **parallel**: `1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2` — the equivalent is **smaller** than the smallest of them.

# Magnetism

Currents and magnets create a **magnetic field** `B` (tesla, T). A charge moving inside `B` feels the **Lorentz force**, perpendicular to its velocity:

```
F = |q|·v·B·sin θ
```

Because the force is perpendicular, it only **bends** the path: the charge moves in a circle of radius

```
r = m·v / (|q|·B)
```

With a crossed electric field, the electric and magnetic forces cancel when `q·E = q·v·B`, that is, `v = E / B`: the **velocity selector** of mass spectrometers.

# Induction: electricity from motion

**Faraday's law:** a **changing** magnetic flux through a loop creates a voltage: `ε = −ΔΦ / Δt`. The minus sign (**Lenz's law**) says the induced current opposes the change. That's how power plants, dynamos, transformers and wireless chargers work.

Maxwell put it all together and found that changing electric and magnetic fields sustain each other and travel at `c = 1/√(μ0·ε0) ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s`: **light is an electromagnetic wave**.

hints: μC is microcoulomb: 1 μC = 10⁻⁶ C.
In Coulomb's law r is squared; in `P = R·I²` it is the current that is squared.
For the radius of the magnetic orbit, convert the result from metres to centimetres (× 100).

fis-10-arrasto-numerico.title: University physics: air resistance and numerical methods
fis-10-arrasto-numerico.theory:
# When the formula runs out

In lesson 1 the range had a closed formula. Just add **air** and it disappears. At everyday speeds the drag force grows with the **square** of the speed and points against it:

```
F_drag = ½·ρ·C·A·v²
```

`ρ` is the air density (~1.2 kg/m³), `C` the shape coefficient (sphere ≈ 0.47), `A` the frontal area. Dividing by the mass, the equation of motion becomes:

```
a = −g·ŷ − k·|v|·v
k = ρ·C·A / (2·m)      (unit: 1/m)
```

The `|v|·v` term **couples** x and y: slowing down horizontally depends on the vertical speed and vice versa. There is no solution in elementary functions — we need a **numerical method**.

# Numerical integration

The idea: step time forward in small steps `dt`, using the derivative to estimate the next state.

## Euler's method

```
while y >= 0:
    v_mod = sqrt(vx*vx + vy*vy)
    ax = -k*v_mod*vx
    ay = -g - k*v_mod*vy
    x, y   = x + vx*dt, y + vy*dt
    vx, vy = vx + ax*dt, vy + ay*dt
    t = t + dt
```

Simple, but the total error is **proportional to dt** (a 1st-order method): to gain one decimal place, 10 times more steps.

## 4th-order Runge–Kutta (RK4)

It computes the derivative at 4 points of the interval (start, two in the middle, end) and takes a weighted average `(k1 + 2·k2 + 2·k3 + k4)/6`. The error falls with **dt⁴**: halving the step makes the result 16 times more accurate. It is what this simulator uses (dt = 0.5 ms).

# What air changes

- **Terminal velocity:** while falling, drag grows until it equals the weight: `k·v² = g` → `v_t = √(g/k)`.
- The range drops a lot, and the **best angle falls below 45°**: climbing high costs time in the air, and the air keeps stealing speed.
- The path is no longer symmetric: the descent is steeper than the climb. The dashed curve shows the same ball in a vacuum.

# Going further: Lagrange's view

In analytical mechanics you don't start from forces but from the **Lagrangian** `L = T − V` (kinetic minus potential energy), written in convenient coordinates `q`. The real motion obeys the Euler–Lagrange equation:

```
d/dt (∂L/∂q') − ∂L/∂q = 0
```

For a pendulum of length `ℓ`, with `q = θ`: `L = m·ℓ²·θ'²/2 + m·g·ℓ·cos θ` gives directly `θ'' = −(g/ℓ)·sin θ` — the equation the oscillations lab solves. Forces that dissipate energy, like drag, don't fit in a `V` and enter as **generalised forces**.

## And when the speed gets close to light?

Newton's mechanics has a limit too: near `c`, special relativity requires the Lorentz factor `γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²)`. Moving clocks run `γ` times slower and momentum becomes `p = γ·m·v`.

## Simulator assumptions

- Quadratic drag with constant `k` (fixed air density and coefficient), no wind and no spin on the ball (no Magnus effect).

Example: 36° at 35.3 m/s (the ball lands near 39.7 m).

fis-11-rotacao.title: Rotation: torque, moment of inertia and rolling
fis-11-rotacao.theory:
# Spinning costs energy too

So far we treated bodies as points. But a wheel, a ball or a planet also **spins**, and rotation has its own versions of Newton's laws:

- **Torque** (the "turning push"): `τ = r · F · sin θ` (N·m). That's why a long wheel wrench loosens bolts the bare hand can't.
- **Moment of inertia** `I` (kg·m²): the "mass" of rotation. It depends on **how** the mass is distributed around the axis: `I = Σ m·r²`.
- **Newton's 2nd law for rotation:** `τ = I · α` (α = angular acceleration, rad/s²).
- **Rotational energy:** `K = ½ · I · ω²`, and **angular momentum** `L = I · ω`.

For symmetric bodies, `I = k · m · R²`, with a factor `k` that comes from an integral over the volume:

- solid sphere: **k = 2/5**
- solid cylinder (or disc): **k = 1/2**
- hollow sphere: **k = 2/3**
- hoop (thin ring): **k = 1** (all the mass is on the rim)

# The race down the ramp

Release a sphere, a cylinder and a hoop from the top of the same ramp. Who arrives first? Rolling **without slipping** (`v = ω·R`), the potential energy turns into translation **and** rotation:

```
m·g·h = ½·m·v² + ½·I·ω² = ½·m·v²·(1 + k)
v = √(2·g·h / (1 + k))        a = g·sin θ / (1 + k)
```

**Mass and radius cancel out!** Only the factor k matters: the more mass far from the axis, the more energy goes into rotation and the **slower** the body goes down. The solid sphere always wins; the hoop always loses. A block sliding without friction (k = 0) would beat them all — but it doesn't roll.

What makes the ball spin is **static friction** at the contact point. It does no work (the contact point is at rest), but it must be large enough: `μ ≥ k·tan θ / (1 + k)`. On a ramp that is too steep and slippery, the ball **slides** instead of rolling.

# Conservation of angular momentum

With no external torque, `L = I·ω` is conserved. A skater who pulls in her arms lowers I and **spins faster**; collapsing stars become pulsars spinning hundreds of times per second.

Before running, compute `a = g·sin θ / (1 + k)` and `t = √(2L/a)` for each shape.
hints: The share of energy in rotation is k / (1 + k): sphere 28.6%, cylinder 33.3%, hollow sphere 40%, hoop 50%.
Mass and radius don't change the time — only the shape (the factor k) matters.

fis-12-fluidos.title: Fluids: pressure, buoyancy and Torricelli's jet
fis-12-fluidos.theory:
# Pressure in a liquid

Pressure is force per area: `p = F / A` (pascal, Pa = N/m²). In a still liquid, pressure **increases with depth**, because each layer holds up the weight of the ones above:

```
p = p0 + ρ·g·h          (hydrostatic law)
```

In water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³), every **10 m** of depth adds ~**1 atmosphere** (≈ 100 kPa). That's why divers feel pain in their ears and submarines need thick hulls.

- **Pascal's principle:** a pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted in full. In a **hydraulic press**, `F1/A1 = F2/A2`: a small piston pushed with little force lifts a car on a large piston.
- **Archimedes' principle:** a submerged body gets an upward **buoyant force** equal to the weight of the liquid it displaces: `E = ρ·g·V`. If the buoyancy beats the weight, it floats.

# Fluids in motion

For an ideal fluid (incompressible, no viscosity) flowing steadily:

- **Continuity:** what goes in comes out. `A1·v1 = A2·v2` — where the pipe narrows, the fluid speeds up (it's the thumb over the end of the hose).
- **Bernoulli:** along a streamline, the energy per volume is conserved:

```
p + ½·ρ·v² + ρ·g·y = constant
```

Where the speed increases, the pressure drops. This explains (in part) the lift of wings and how carburetors and the Venturi tube work.

# Torricelli's jet

Drill a hole in the side of a tank, at a depth `h` below the surface. Applying Bernoulli between the surface (still, at atmospheric pressure) and the hole (also at atmospheric pressure):

```
v = √(2·g·h)
```

The water leaves at the same speed it would have if it **fell** from height h! If the hole is at a height `y` above the floor, the jet is a **horizontal launch**: it falls in `t = √(2y/g)` and reaches

```
x = v·t = 2·√(h·y)
```

Note that `h·y` is the same if you swap h and y: **two different holes hit the same spot**. The maximum range is when the hole is at half the water's height (h = y), and it equals the height of the water column exactly.

Use `x = 2·√(h·y)` with `h + y = 1 m`: two heights hit the bucket — only one of them has the required speed.
hints: The roots are y = 0.2 m and y = 0.8 m. Compute v = √(2·g·h) for each.
The low hole is deeper (h = 0.8 m) and the jet leaves faster: √(2·9.81·0.8) ≈ 3.96 m/s.

The water leaves at at least 3 m/s

questions.explanation: Pascal: F2 = F1 · A2 / A1 = 100 · 500 / 10 = 5000 N. But the small piston has to move 50 times farther: energy is conserved.

fis-13-ondas-som.title: Waves and sound: vibrating strings and tuning
fis-13-ondas-som.theory:
# What is a wave

A wave carries **energy**, not matter: the string goes up and down, but doesn't travel. Every periodic wave has:

- a **wavelength** λ (m), a **frequency** f (Hz) and a **speed** `v = λ·f`.

**Sound** is a **longitudinal** pressure wave in air, at ~**343 m/s** at 20 °C. We hear from ~20 Hz to ~20 000 Hz.

# The string of an instrument

On a stretched string, the wave speed depends on the **tension** T and the **linear density** μ (mass per meter):

```
v = √(T / μ)
```

Fixed at both ends, the string can only vibrate in patterns where the ends stay still (**nodes**): **standing waves**. A whole number of half-waves fits in the length L:

```
λn = 2L / n        fn = n · v / (2L) = (n / 2L) · √(T/μ)
```

- n = 1 is the **fundamental** (the note we hear); n = 2, 3… are the **harmonics**, whole multiples of it. The mix of harmonics is the **timbre**: that's why a violin and a flute playing the same note sound different.
- **Tuning** means changing T (the tuning peg); **pressing a finger** shortens L and raises the note; **thick** strings (larger μ) are low.

# Intensity and decibels

The ear perceives intensities from 10⁻¹² W/m² up to ~1 W/m². To fit that range, we use a **logarithmic** scale:

```
β = 10 · log10(I / I0)   [dB]
```

Every **×10** in intensity adds **10 dB**; ×100 adds 20 dB.

# Beats and the Doppler effect

- Two close notes (440 and 444 Hz) played together make the sound "pulse" with `fbeat = |f1 − f2|` = 4 times per second. Musicians tune until the beats disappear.
- **Doppler:** a source **approaching** sounds higher; moving away, lower. With the source at `vs` and the listener at rest: `f' = f · v / (v − vs)` (approaching).
fis-13-ondas-som.task: A violin string has **L = 32.5 cm** and **μ = 0.6 g/m** (locked). Set the **tension** so the **fundamental** note (n = 1) is the **A at 440 Hz** (between 438 and 442 Hz). Compute it first: `T = μ · (2·L·f)²`.
hints: Convert: μ = 0.6 g/m = 0.0006 kg/m; L = 0.325 m.
The required speed is v = 2·L·f = 2 · 0.325 · 440 = 286 m/s.
T = μ·v² = 0.0006 · 286² ≈ 49.1 N. Keep the harmonic at n = 1.
goals: Frequency between 438 and 442 Hz
Vibrating in the fundamental (n = 1)

questions.prompt: What is the wavelength, in air (v = 343 m/s), of the **440 Hz** A?
Two tuning forks, of **440 Hz** and **444 Hz**, sound together. How many beats per second do you hear?
questions.explanation: fbeat = |444 − 440| = 4 Hz: the volume rises and falls 4 times per second.

questions.prompt: The intensity of a sound becomes **100 times** larger. How many decibels does it gain?
An ambulance with a **700 Hz** siren approaches you at **20 m/s** (sound at 343 m/s). What frequency do you hear?
questions.explanation: f' = f · v / (v − vs) = 700 · 343 / 323 ≈ 743.3 Hz — higher. When it passes and moves away, it drops to 700 · 343 / 363 ≈ 661 Hz.

fis-14-calor.title: Heat: calorimetry, phase changes and heat transfer
fis-14-calor.theory:
# Temperature is not heat

**Temperature** measures the average agitation of the molecules (in kelvin: `T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15`). **Heat** is energy **in transit** because of a temperature difference — always from the hotter to the colder.

# Sensible and latent heat

- **Sensible heat** changes the temperature: `Q = m · c · ΔT`. The **specific heat** c of water is huge, **4186 J/(kg·K)** — that's why the sea is slow to warm up and regulates the climate of coastal cities.
- **Latent heat** changes the **phase** without changing the temperature: `Q = m · L`. To melt ice at 0 °C, `Lf = 334 kJ/kg`; to boil water at 100 °C, `Lv = 2260 kJ/kg`. While the ice melts, the energy goes into **breaking the bonds** between molecules, and the thermometer stays at 0 °C.

# Calorimetry

In an insulated container, the heat one body loses is what the other gains: `Σ Q = 0`. Mixing masses of water m1 (at T1) and m2 (at T2):

```
Tf = (m1·T1 + m2·T2) / (m1 + m2)
```

# The three ways heat travels

- **Conduction:** from molecule to molecule, through a material. Fourier's law: `P = k · A · ΔT / L` (k = conductivity: copper ~400, glass ~0.8, styrofoam ~0.03 W/(m·K)). Thick, insulating walls conduct less.
- **Convection:** the hot fluid, less dense, **rises** and carries the heat with it — currents in the air, in the water in a pot, in winds and ocean currents.
- **Radiation:** electromagnetic waves (infrared); it works even in a **vacuum** (that's how the Sun warms us). Stefan–Boltzmann law:

```
P = ε · σ · A · T⁴        σ = 5.67×10⁻⁸ W/(m²·K⁴)
```

T is in **kelvin** and to the **fourth power**: doubling the absolute temperature multiplies the radiation by 16. A body also **absorbs** radiation from its surroundings, so the net loss is `ε·σ·A·(T⁴ − Tsurr⁴)`.

A thermos fights all three: a vacuum between the walls (no conduction or convection) and mirrored walls (little radiation).

hints: In Q = m·c·ΔT, ΔT in °C or in K gives the same number; answer in kJ when asked (÷ 1000).

questions.explanation: P = k·A·ΔT / L = 0.8 · 2 · 20 / 0.004 = 8000 W. That's why double-glazed windows (with still air in between) save so much energy.

Because the energy received goes into breaking the bonds of the solid (latent heat)

Because the thermometer can't measure below the water
questions.explanation: During a phase change, the heat received is latent heat: it changes how the molecules are organized, not their average agitation.

options: By convection: the warm air rises, the cold air sinks and a current forms
Through the vacuum between the molecules
questions.explanation: Heated air becomes less dense and rises; cold air sinks near the heater and gets heated: a convection current. That's why heaters go low and air conditioners go high.

fis-15-kepler-hohmann.title: Gravitation: Kepler's laws and the Hohmann transfer
fis-15-kepler-hohmann.theory:
# Kepler's laws

Analyzing Tycho Brahe's observations, Kepler discovered three laws that Newton later explained with gravitation:

1. Orbits are **ellipses** with the planet (or star) at one of the **foci**.
2. The planet–satellite line sweeps **equal areas in equal times**: the satellite is fastest at **periapsis** (closest point) and slowest at **apoapsis** (farthest). It is conservation of angular momentum.
3. `T² = (4π² / GM) · a³`: the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the **semi-major axis** `a = (rp + ra) / 2`.

# Energy and the vis-viva equation

The energy of an orbit depends only on `a`: `E = −G·M·m / (2a)`. From it comes **vis-viva**, the most useful equation in astronautics:

```
v² = μ · (2/r − 1/a)          μ = G·M  (Earth: 398 600 km³/s²)
```

- circular orbit (a = r): `v = √(μ/r)`
- escape (a → ∞): `v = √(2μ/r)`

# The Hohmann transfer

How do you take a satellite from a low orbit (400 km) to **geostationary orbit** (35 786 km altitude, period of one sidereal day)? The most economical maneuver between two circular orbits, found by Walter Hohmann in 1925, uses **half an ellipse** that touches both:

1. **1st burn** (at periapsis, at 400 km): speed up from `√(μ/r1)` to the speed of the transfer ellipse, with `a = (r1 + r2)/2`. The satellite climbs.
2. **Half a lap** of unpowered "gliding": half the period of the ellipse.
3. **2nd burn** (at apoapsis, at 35 786 km): speed up again to `√(μ/r2)` and circularize.

With r1 = 6771 km and r2 = 42 157 km: a = 24 464 km, and vis-viva gives the speed at periapsis:

```
vp = √(398600 · (2/6771 − 1/24464)) ≈ 10.07 km/s
```

fis-16-amortecimento.title: Damped oscillations: critical damping
fis-16-amortecimento.theory:
# The spring that loses energy

A real oscillator loses energy: friction, air resistance, a damper. The most used model is a **viscous** force, proportional to velocity: `F = −b·v`. The equation of motion becomes a **2nd-order differential equation**:

```
m·x'' + b·x' + k·x = 0
```

Trying solutions of the form `x = e^(s·t)`, we get `m·s² + b·s + k = 0`. Everything depends on the **damping ratio**:

```
ζ = b / (2·√(k·m))        ω0 = √(k/m)
```

# Three regimes

- **Underdamped (ζ < 1):** it oscillates with an amplitude that decays as `e^(−ζ·ω0·t)`, at a slightly lower frequency: `ωd = ω0·√(1 − ζ²)`. It goes past the equilibrium point: the **overshoot** is `e^(−π·ζ/√(1−ζ²))` of the amplitude.
- **Critical (ζ = 1, b = 2·√(k·m)):** the root is double and `x = A·(1 + ω0·t)·e^(−ω0·t)`. It **doesn't oscillate** and returns to equilibrium **as fast as possible** without passing it.
- **Overdamped (ζ > 1):** it doesn't oscillate either, but returns **slowly**, "bogged down" by the damping.

# Where it matters

- **Car suspension:** close to critical — no bouncing after a pothole, but not too stiff.
- **Spring-loaded doors** and instrument needles: critical, to stop fast without slamming back.
- **Control (PID):** a well-tuned controller makes the system respond like an almost critical oscillator — it's the same problem as the PID lesson in the Arduino track.
- **Buildings and bridges:** tuned mass dampers take energy out of oscillations caused by wind and earthquakes.

# Settling time

Engineers measure how fast the system "calms down" by the **settling time**: the instant after which |x| stays below **2%** of the initial amplitude forever. With little damping it is long (it oscillates a lot); with too much damping, too (it returns slowly); the minimum is near critical.

hints: With b much smaller it oscillates and overshoots; with b much larger it returns too slowly.

fis-17-espectrometro.title: Magnetic field: the mass spectrometer
fis-17-espectrometro.theory:
# Weighing atoms one by one

How do you measure the mass of a single atom? And separate carbon-14 (radioactive, used to date fossils) from carbon-12, if chemically they are identical? The **mass spectrometer** does it with electric and magnetic fields.

# 1. Accelerate with an electric field

The ion (charge q, mass m) starts at rest and crosses a potential difference V. The electric field does work `q·V`, which becomes kinetic energy:

```
q·V = ½·m·v²     →     v = √(2·q·V / m)
```

Lighter ions come out faster. The energy of one elementary charge accelerated through 1 V is **1 electronvolt** (1 eV = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ J).

# 2. Bend with a magnetic field

Inside a field **B** perpendicular to the velocity, the **Lorentz force** `F = q·v·B` is always perpendicular to the motion: it doesn't change the speed, only the direction. The ion moves in **uniform circular motion**, and the magnetic force is the centripetal force:

```
q·v·B = m·v² / r     →     r = m·v / (q·B)
```

Putting both stages together:

```
r = (1/B) · √(2·m·V / q)
```

The radius grows with the **square root of the mass**. After half a turn, the ion hits the detector at a distance **2r** from the entrance: each mass lands in a different place, like the colors of a rainbow — hence "spectrum".

# The period doesn't depend on the speed

The time of one turn is `T = 2π·m / (q·B)`, with no v! Faster ions make larger circles, but at the same frequency — the **cyclotron frequency**. It is the principle of the **cyclotron** accelerator and of magnetic resonance.

# Applications

Carbon-14 dating (with accelerator mass spectrometers), doping control, pollutant analysis, uranium isotope separation (Manhattan Project) and protein identification in biology.

Masses: 1 u = 1.6605×10⁻²⁷ kg; ¹²C = 12 u, ¹⁴C = 14.0032 u; ion charge = +e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C.

fis-18-inducao.title: Electromagnetic induction: generators and transformers
fis-18-inducao.theory:
# Magnetic flux

The **magnetic flux** through a loop measures "how many field lines" cross it:

```
Φ = B · A · cos θ       (weber, Wb = T·m²)
```

# Faraday–Lenz law

A voltage (electromotive force, **emf**) appears in a coil of N turns whenever the flux **changes**:

```
ε = −N · ΔΦ / Δt
```

The flux can change because B changes (a magnet approaching), because the area changes, or because the angle changes (the loop spins). The minus sign is **Lenz's law**: the induced current creates a field that **opposes the change** that created it. If it weren't so, energy would come out of nothing. That's why a magnet dropped inside a copper tube falls slowly (eddy currents) — the same principle as the electromagnetic brakes of trains.

# Motional emf

A rod of length L moving at speed v, perpendicular to a field B, has its charges pushed by the Lorentz force: `ε = B · L · v`.

# The generator

A coil of N turns and area A spinning with angular speed ω in a field B has `Φ = B·A·cos(ωt)`. Taking the derivative:

```
ε(t) = N · B · A · ω · sin(ωt)        peak: ε0 = N·B·A·ω
```

It is a sinusoidal **alternating** voltage: the origin of the alternating current from power plants (60 Hz in Brazil and the US, ω = 2π·60 ≈ 377 rad/s).

# The transformer

Two coils on the same iron core: the alternating current in the primary creates a changing flux that induces a voltage in the secondary. Since the flux is the same:

```
Vs / Vp = Ns / Np        and (ideal)  Vp·Ip = Vs·Is
```

Transformers only work with **alternating** current (with direct current there is no change in flux). They allow **transmitting power at high voltage**: for the same power, the current is lower, and the loss in the wires `P = R·I²` drops with the square of the current.

# Energy in the field

A coil (inductor, L in henries) carrying current I stores energy in its magnetic field: `U = ½·L·I²`.

fis-19-relatividade.title: Special relativity: time, space and energy
fis-19-relatividade.theory:
# The two postulates

In 1905, Einstein started from two ideas:

1. The laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame (without acceleration).
2. The speed of light in vacuum, **c ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s**, is the same for all observers, no matter how they move.

The second is strange: if you run after a light beam, it keeps moving away at c. For that to work, **time and space** must change from observer to observer.

# The Lorentz factor

```
γ = 1 / √(1 − v²/c²)
```

At everyday speeds γ ≈ 1 (at 300 m/s, γ − 1 ≈ 5×10⁻¹³). Close to c, it shoots up: γ = 1.25 at 0.6c, 1.67 at 0.8c, ~10 at 0.995c.

- **Time dilation:** a moving clock runs slower: `Δt = γ·Δt0` (Δt0 = **proper time**, measured in the clock's own frame).
- **Length contraction:** a moving object is shorter along its motion: `L = L0 / γ`.
- **Simultaneity is relative:** two events simultaneous for one observer may not be for another.

# The muon proof

Cosmic rays create **muons** ~15 km up. They live **2.2 μs** on average; even at nearly c, without relativity they would travel only ~660 m before decaying — and almost none would reach the ground. But many do! For us, their clock runs γ times slower; for them, the atmosphere is contracted. Both descriptions give the same result.

# Adding velocities

Velocities don't simply add. A ship moving at u launches a probe at v' (relative to the ship):

```
v = (u + v') / (1 + u·v'/c²)
```

It never exceeds c: 0.5c "plus" 0.5c gives 0.8c.

# E = mc²

Mass is energy: `E0 = m·c²`. The total energy of a moving body is `E = γ·m·c²`. Since c² is enormous, one gram of mass equals 9×10¹³ J — more than the Hiroshima bomb. In nuclear plants and in the Sun, a small fraction of the mass turns into energy.

**GPS** has to correct the satellites' clocks for special relativity (they move) and general relativity (they are farther from the Earth): without that, it would drift ~10 km per day.

fis-20-quantica.title: Quantum physics: photons, matter waves and the atom
fis-20-quantica.theory:
# Light comes in packets

In 1900, Planck explained the radiation of hot bodies by assuming energy is exchanged in **packets**. Einstein (1905) took the idea seriously: light is made of **photons**, each with energy

```
E = h·f = h·c / λ        h = 6.626×10⁻³⁴ J·s
```

A handy shortcut: `h·c ≈ 1240 eV·nm`, so a 500 nm (green) photon has 1240/500 = 2.48 eV.

# The photoelectric effect

Light knocks electrons out of a metal — but only if **each photon** has enough energy to overcome the metal's **work function** W:

```
Kmax = h·f − W
```

Very strong red light knocks out nothing; weak ultraviolet does. The intensity only changes **how many** electrons come out, not the energy of each one. That (and not relativity) is what won Einstein the Nobel Prize.

# Matter waves

De Broglie (1924) proposed the reverse: particles are waves too, with

```
λ = h / p = h / (m·v)
```

An electron accelerated through V volts has `p = √(2·m·e·V)`. With 100 V, λ ≈ 0.12 nm — the size of atoms, which is why electrons **diffract** in crystals and electron microscopes see details light can't reach.

# The Bohr atom

In hydrogen, the electron can only have energies `En = −13.6 eV / n²`. When it drops from one level to another, it emits a photon with exactly the energy difference. The drop from n = 3 to n = 2 gives the red **Hα** line (656 nm), which colors nebulae. Each element has its own lines: that's how we know what stars are made of.

# Uncertainty and duality

- **Heisenberg:** `Δx · Δp ≥ ħ/2` (ħ = h/2π = 1.055×10⁻³⁴ J·s). The more confined an electron is, the more uncertain its velocity — which is why the atom doesn't collapse.
- **Double slit:** electrons sent **one at a time** slowly build up an **interference** pattern: each behaves as a wave that goes through both slits, but is detected as a particle at one point.
- **Tunneling:** a particle can cross a barrier that, classically, it wouldn't have the energy to jump over. It explains alpha decay and is used in scanning tunneling microscopes and flash memory.

hints: Photon energy in eV: E = 1240 / λ(nm).
